title: Bless, O my soul (Berakhot 10a)
hookLine: David says "Bless the LORD, O my soul" five times, for five stages of life
tomorrow: what did the sages pray when nobody handed them the words?
last: A WEEK OF HANDS AND MERCY.

lines: BLESS THE LORD, O MY SOUL.
cards: Some songs repeat one line so many times it should get old, and somehow it lands harder every time. King David has a line like that: Bless the LORD, O my soul. Across the Psalms he says it five times.
Right after Hezekiah's story, Berakhot asks the obvious question. Why five?

teach.b: One answer comes in Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's name: David said it once for each of the five worlds he lived in.

teach.h: THE WOMB, THE STARS, THE BREAST.
teach.b: In his mother's womb. When he came out into the world and looked up at the stars. When he nursed at his mother's breast.

teach.h: THE WICKED FALL, THE LAST DAY.
teach.b: When he saw the wicked fall. And when he looked toward the day of his death. Five stages of a life, and the same line at every one.
The psalm opens: "Bless the LORD, O my soul; and all that is within me, bless His holy name."
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this reading, David blesses God before he was even born, and again facing his own death.

teach.h: IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE GOOD PART.
teach.b: The line doesn't wait for the good chapter. It goes with him through all of them.
That's the word: bless. Not a feeling you wait for, but a line you bring into each stage, the hard ones from this week too: a sickbed, a small apartment, a sword on the neck.

how: Psalm 104, which opens 'Bless the LORD, O my soul', is said in many communities on Rosh Chodesh, the start of a new month, and some say it on Shabbat afternoons in the winter.

o: to sprinkle water on someone as a sign of welcome
to ask God to keep you safe from all harm
to praise and thank God with your whole self

games.q: five worlds, one line — tap the pairs.

s: David says 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' just once, at the start of a psalm
Berakhot counts five times across the Psalms, and asks why.
in one reading, David blesses God even in his mother's womb
the first of five worlds, in Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi's name.
all five stages are happy ones
they include seeing the wicked fall and looking toward the day of death.

games.q: your aunt says she'll start counting her blessings once this rough year is over. what does Berakhot 10a suggest?
o: David blessed at every stage, hard ones too; it doesn't wait for the good chapter.
wait; a blessing only means something when life is going well.
bless only the past; the present is too close to see clearly yet.
games.why: five stages, from before birth to the day of death, and the same line at each one. the blessing goes with David through all of them.

practice: Count back through the stages of your life so far on your fingers: small child, school, now, and whatever came between. Stop on one stage, maybe a hard one, and find one thing in it you're grateful for.
If you pray, you can say David's line over it; if not, simply hold it with thanks for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Bless. David's five-times line, Bless the LORD, O my soul, said at every stage of a life.

orig.note: Hebrew: bless, O my soul, the opening of Psalms 103 and 104.

carryVoice: Your line: bless, O my soul, in every stage, the hard ones too. Eleven days into Berakhot, and counting.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a (five times 'Bless the LORD, O my soul'; Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: five worlds David lived in)

sources.q: Bless the LORD, O my soul; and all that is within me, bless His holy name.
